manifest

/MAN-uh-fest/ - the stress falls on MAN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Manifest means easily understandable, obvious.

The cellist's stage fright was manifest in the first bars, then gone by the second page.

Worked Example

By the third lap the champion's exhaustion was manifest to the whole stadium: the stride shortened, the shoulders climbed, and the split times on the board only confirmed what every eye had already seen.

Manifest fits because the exhaustion showed itself in outward signs anyone could read — no inference needed. A feeling you deduce from hints is merely detectable; one written across the body in plain view is manifest.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

evident: Evident means plain to see — the ordinary word for what a fair look at the facts takes in. Manifest is stronger and more formal: the thing displays itself so openly that no looking is really required. A limp makes an injury evident; agony written across a face is manifest.

unmistakable: Unmistakable means impossible to read as anything else — once seen, it allows only a single interpretation. Manifest is about display: the feeling or fact shows itself openly, worn in plain sight. Something can be manifest and still get misread; unmistakable adds that no misreading is possible at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

veiled: covered over, only hinted at

imperceptible: too slight to notice at all

Where it sits · how impossible it is to miss — noticeable → manifest → undeniable

noticeable vs. manifest: Noticeable means you can spot it if you look; it stops short of manifest, which no one could miss.

undeniable vs. manifest: Undeniable goes further than manifest — not merely plain to see, but impossible to argue against.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mani-

Root — mani-: hand (Latin manus)

Root — -fest

Root — -fest: gripped, struck (Latin -festus)

Put it together

Put it together: Mani- (hand) + -fest (gripped) = graspable by hand. Latin manifestus described what you could seize with your fingers — evidence so solid you could literally hold it — and the word still means truths and feelings so plain you could all but touch them.

Use the root in a new word: manuscript

Use the root in a new word: manuscript: The archive paid a fortune for the composer's original manuscript, ink smudges and all.

Word Choice

formal

Manifest is the formal word for feelings and facts worn in plain view — grief, relief, danger. This card teaches the adjective; be ready to recognize the same spelling as a noun (a ship's cargo manifest) and a verb (symptoms manifest), which the SAT also likes. Beside this unit's limpid, the line is: limpid is the see-through medium, manifest the fact standing in full sight.
